> Verify that the application protects against Server‑side Request Forgery
(SSRF) attacks, by validating untrusted data against an allowlist of protocols,
domains, paths and ports and sanitizing potentially dangerous characters
before using the data to call another service.

### "Sanitizing Potentially Dangerous Characters" 
* What characters are considered as "dangerous'?
* Why sanitization is important? I am having difficulty find the information about sanitization for SSRF, I have referered Below URL:

| Reference Site| Comment |
| -------- | ------- |
| [Cheatsheet ](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Server_Side_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html)| Missing Sanitization Word    |
| [OWASP TOP 10 SSRF](https://owasp.org/Top10/A10_2021-Server-Side_Request_Forgery_%28SSRF%29/) | Found 'Sanitize' word only.    |
| [Portswigger    ](https://portswigger.net/web-security/ssrf)| Missing Sanitization Word |
| [Accunetix ](https://www.acunetix.com/blog/articles/server-side-request-forgery-vulnerability/)| Missing Sanitization Word |
| [SSRF Bible Cheatsheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/assets/Server_Side_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet_SSRF_Bible.pdf) | Missing Sanitization Word |
| [Blackhat ](https://www.blackhat.com/docs/us-17/thursday/us-17-Tsai-A-New-Era-Of-SSRF-Exploiting-URL-Parser-In-Trending-Programming-Languages.pdf)| Missing Sanitization Word |


As far as I know, the sanitization is not the primary defense. the requirement doesn’t specify how granular or strict the allow list should be and also other important terms are missing in the requirement.

comments.body:
I can see why you made this comment. If you use an allow list, then sanitizing potentially dangerous characters
before using the data to call another service is a good idea. Usually, it's not sanitization, it's validation. 

Sanitization implies cleaning data, and then using it, which is rarely a good idea for SSRF defense. I would change this requirement to say something like:

_Verify that the application protects against Server‑Side Request Forgery (SSRF) attacks, by validating untrusted data against an allowlist of protocols, domains, paths and  potentially dangerous characters before using the data to call another service._
I think Jim's suggestion makes sense.

This proposed wording is not anymore sanitization.

Also, how it is different from 13.2.4?
| # | Description | Level |
| :---: | :--- | :---: |
| **13.2.4** | Verify that an allowlist is used to define the external resources or systems with which the application is permitted to communicate (e.g., for outbound requests, data loads, or file access). This allowlist can be implemented at the application layer, web server, firewall, or a combination of different layers. | 2 |

Fair point Elar. My point is, if we want a SSRF specific requirement, one of the main controls is proper validation of untrusted URL's. And doing URL validation is actually quite difficult to get right. I personally like this as a separate requirement but I can understand why you would not due to 13.2.4.

The OAuth standard changes due to the challenges of URL validation and now suggest allow-list validation of URL's vs RegEx.

I am not sure if we want to go into this detail, but those are the facts. :)
I did not criticize the proposal content, just pointed out the side-effects. We just can not update the current requirement to proposed text, it will contain the conflicts I pointed out.

"sanitizing potentially dangerous characters" is this wrong control as the OP stated and I agree we need to drop it from the requirement so it's accurate. It is not right now. In fact, trying to "sanitize" an invalid URL is dangerous.

So we need to change this or drop it if we seek accuracy.

> In fact, trying to "sanitize" an invalid URL is dangerous.

I'd even say sanitization is always dangerous. It's a naive approach that (like blacklists) is near-impossible to provide 100% coverage, and even then it leads to unpredictable side-effects because it corrupts the input data.

I don't know how many times I need to write it, but one more time

  * first - when we talk about sanitization, we talk about allow-list patterns - we allow only the accepted and known-to-be-safe pattern
  * second - if step 1 is done, the difference between input validation and sanitization is only the question - is it allowed to automatically modify user-input, or do we need to let the user know that the input was not valid and the user needs to change it (instead of automatic modification)

> > In fact, trying to "sanitize" an invalid URL is dangerous.
> 
> I'd even say sanitization is always dangerous. It's a naive approach that (like blacklists) is near-impossible to provide 100% coverage, and even then it leads to unpredictable side-effects because it corrupts the input data.

See also #3335 @narfbg

I've done some analysis on the history of this requirement and I agree that the sanitization language needs to go.

**TL;DR:** This requirement ended up in the Sanitization section by historical accident and the sanitization wording was added to justify that placement. I think we should remove V1.3.6 entirely and fold the SSRF-specific user-input concern into V13.2.4, which already covers allowlisting outbound communications. Proposed updated V13.2.4:

"_Verify that an allowlist is used to define the external resources or systems with which the application is permitted to communicate (e.g., for outbound requests, data loads, or file access). Any user-supplied data that is used to construct or influence outbound requests, such as URLs, hostnames, or IP addresses should be subject to this. This allowlist can be implemented at the application layer, web server, firewall, or a combination of different layers_"

---

<details>
<summary>Full analysis</summary>

### How it ended up in the Sanitization section

It was moved into "Sanitization and Sandboxing" (V5.2) during a bulk restructuring in February 2019 ([`2e561634`](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/commit/2e561634)) without a clear rationale for that specific section. When I rewrote it in #2115/#2125, I added "sanitizing potentially dangerous characters" partly to justify the section placement — but as this issue shows, that justification doesn't hold up. I even noted at the time that "I don't like sanitization as I don't think it is exactly what is being done."

### The overlap with V13.2

As @elarlang pointed out, if we drop the sanitization language, this overlaps significantly with V13.2.4 and V13.2.5:

| # | Description | Level |
| :---: | :--- | :---: |
| **13.2.4** | Verify that an allowlist is used to define the external resources or systems with which the application is permitted to communicate (e.g., for outbound requests, data loads, or file access). This allowlist can be implemented at the application layer, web server, firewall, or a combination of different layers. | 2 |
| **13.2.5** | Verify that the web or application server is configured with an allowlist of resources or systems to which the server can send requests or load data or files from. | 2 |

A sanitization-free V1.3.6 would essentially be "validate user-controlled URLs against an allowlist before making outbound requests" — which is an application-layer implementation of V13.2.4.

### Proposal

Remove V1.3.6 and strengthen V13.2.4 to explicitly cover the user-input case:

"_Verify that an allowlist is used to define the external resources or systems with which the application is permitted to communicate (e.g., for outbound requests, data loads, or file access). Any user-supplied data that is used to construct or influence outbound requests, such as URLs, hostnames, or IP addresses should be subject to this. This allowlist can be implemented at the application layer, web server, firewall, or a combination of different layers_"

This preserves the SSRF-specific URL validation concern @jmanico values, keeps the defense-in-depth layering with V13.2.5 (server config), and eliminates the inaccurate sanitization framing raised by @ajayojha .

</details>

> * first - when we talk about sanitization, we talk about allow-list patterns - we allow only the accepted and known-to-be-safe pattern

That is not how HTML sanitizers (or sanitizers in general) work. They are much more complex.

**Sanitizers modify data**, validators reject data, encoders preserve data and just change the format to be safe for that context. 

_The fact that sanitizers actually modify data significantly is why they have a history of being dangerous and largely should be avoided._ HTML sanitizers are only of the few special cases where sanitization is necessary.

> I've done some analysis on the history of this requirement and I agree that the sanitization language needs to go.
> 
> **TL;DR:** This requirement ended up in the Sanitization section by historical accident and the sanitization wording was added to justify that placement. I think we should remove V1.3.6 entirely and fold the SSRF-specific user-input concern into V13.2.4, which already covers allowlisting outbound communications. Proposed updated V13.2.4:
> 
> "_Verify that an allowlist is used to define the external resources or systems with which the application is permitted to communicate (e.g., for outbound requests, data loads, or file access). Any user-supplied data that is used to construct or influence outbound requests, such as URLs, hostnames, or IP addresses should be subject to this. This allowlist can be implemented at the application layer, web server, firewall, or a combination of different layers_"
> 
> Full analysis

I like this direction!
@elarlang any thoughts on this: https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/3244#issuecomment-3940672689

I don't have a good proposal for this, but I would like to have separate requirement(s) for the application (business) logic (V1 or V2) and for the configuration (V13).

V13 is a general 2nd layer of defense that should be mainly done with configuration - it defines **globally** to which external resources the application can communicate.

V1 or V2 requirement should be defined in the application logic to which external resources it can communicate for **this specific functionality** as a 1st layer of defense.

> I don't have a good proposal for this, but I would like to have separate requirement(s) for the application (business) logic (V1 or V2) and for the configuration (V13).
> 
> V13 is a general 2nd layer of defense that should be mainly done with configuration - it defines **globally** to which external resources the application can communicate.
> 
> V1 or V2 requirement should be defined in the application logic to which external resources it can communicate for **this specific functionality** as a 1st layer of defense.

This is good stuff. I would suggest we add some of it to the section header of https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/blob/master/5.0/en/0x22-V13-Configuration.md and similar for clarity.

@elarlang I can see the logic in having separate layers, but I'm struggling to see what the V1/V2 requirement would actually say that is clearly distinct from V13.2.4.

V13.2.4 already says the allowlist "can be implemented at the application layer, web server, firewall, or a combination of different layers", so it already covers application-level enforcement. If we add a separate V1 or V2 requirement for "validate user-supplied data against an allowlist before making outbound requests", how is that meaningfully different from "use an allowlist for outbound communications, implemented at the application layer"?

The only distinction I can see is **granularity**: V13.2.4 defines a global policy ("these are all the external services this application is allowed to talk to"), while a V1/V2 requirement would define a per-feature policy ("for this specific functionality, these are the permitted destinations"). That is a real and valuable distinction, but is it what you had in mind?

Could you (or @jmanico) propose concrete wording or at least more direction for both requirements? I think that would make it much clearer whether the split works or whether we end up with two requirements that say essentially the same thing.

To be clear, I am happy to go with a two-requirement approach if we can articulate a clean split. I just want to avoid having two requirements where auditors and developers can't tell the difference and might actually end up being implemented by the same control.

My only concern is how we use the word "sanitize" which is, I believe, incorrect in the current requirement. I would suggest we audit all uses of the word "sanitize" since it's quite dangerous per https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/3244#issuecomment-3940619235 and others.

@jmanico I have made an attempt to clear this up here in a way that I hope will work for all the requirements in this section: https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/3335#issuecomment-3984248767

@elarlang let me know your thoughts

> That is a real and valuable distinction, but is it what you had in mind?

yes.

Separate requirements gives some clear "actionable" information but as I said, I don't have a clear proposal to solve this.

Thanks @elarlang for confirming. Let me try to draft wording for both requirements so we can see if the split works in practice. I'm not fully convinced it will hold up as two clearly distinct requirements, but the best way to find out is to try.

**Proposed V1 requirement** (replacing V1.3.6, possibly renumbered depending on #3335 outcomes):

"_Verify that, where the application uses user-supplied data to construct or influence outbound requests (such as URLs, hostnames, or IP addresses), the permitted destinations for that specific functionality are validated against an allowlist._"

**Proposed updated V13.2.4:**

"_Verify that an allowlist is used to define, at a global level, the external resources or systems with which the application is permitted to communicate (e.g., for outbound requests, data loads, or file access). This allowlist can be implemented at the web server, firewall, or a combination of different layers._"

The intended distinction: the V1 requirement is about **application code validating per-feature** (e.g., "for this webhook callback, only allow verified domains"), while V13.2.4 is about **infrastructure configuration restricting globally** (e.g., "this server may only make outbound connections to services X, Y, Z"). I removed "application layer" from V13.2.4 to try and make the boundary cleaner.

That said, I'm still not sure an auditor could reliably distinguish these two in practice, or that they wouldn't end up being satisfied by the same control. If we can't get wording that makes the distinction clear and testable, I'd prefer to fall back to my earlier proposal of merging the user-input concern into V13.2.4 (https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/3244#issuecomment-3940672689).

Either way, the "sanitizing potentially dangerous characters" language goes. The broader sanitization discussion is tracked in #3335.

@elarlang @jmanico, does this split work for you, or should we go with the single-requirement approach?

For me, it is clear, but I'm not the best audience to validate it, as I proposed the change myself and know the need and the background for it.

For 1.3.6 - for non-breaking change, we can update the wording but keep the requirement (incorrectly) in the same section till major/minor release.

For breaking-change and for the section change, as we make 1.3.6 (more) clearly as 1st layer of defense, we may want to consider change from L2 to L1.

For 13.2.4 - I think we can just have a wording update and it's a non-breaking change. It may feel that the requirement moves towards L3 as "extra step", but it is really important 2nd layer of defense to make communication from the application to outside harder/impossible if there is already some issue in the application. The point is - even if the 1.3.6 is satisfied, 13.2.4 is required to have general protection - a vulnerability or possibility to make requests to outside may come from functionality that is not meant to make requests and is not subject to 1.3.6 verification.

Not fan of it - but if it is needed, we can write a line into section text to explain that.

To be clear, what new section are you proposing? I am not sure I want to start messing with levels. To be honest I am still struggling with the need to for two requirements or the difference between them.

> To be clear, what new section are you proposing? I am not sure I want to start messing with levels. To be honest I am still struggling with the need to for two requirements or the difference between them.

First, as I mentioned, for patch release I would keep it where it is, although the wording will not match with the section title.

For minor/major, I think it may fit to "V15.3 Defensive Coding". For example, it is quite related with 15.3.2 as well:
> v5.0.0-15.3.2 Verify that where the application backend makes calls to external URLs, it is configured to not follow redirects unless it is intended functionality.

Thanks @elarlang, V15.3 Defensive Coding does seem like a reasonable home for the application-level requirement, given the overlap with 15.3.2 (not following redirects on external URL calls).

Let me try to summarise where I think we've landed. Whether wording changes go into a patch or minor release depends on whether the change modifies what is necessary to comply with the requirement. A section move can only happen in a major release.

### What we agree on

1. The current V1.3.6 wording is problematic, specifically the "sanitizing potentially dangerous characters" language in the SSRF context.
2. We want two separate requirements: one for **per-feature application-level** allowlisting of outbound destinations (1st layer of defense), and one for **global** allowlisting (2nd layer of defense, V13.2.4).

### Proposed changes

**V1.3.6** (kept in V1.3 for now, even though the fit is imperfect):

"_Verify that, where the application uses user-supplied data to construct or influence outbound requests (such as URLs, hostnames, or IP addresses), the permitted destinations for that specific functionality are validated against an allowlist._"

Note: the exact handling of the word "sanitization" in the V1.3 section depends on the outcome of #3335. The key change here is removing the SSRF-specific sanitization language and refocusing on per-feature allowlist validation. Since this changes what is needed to comply, this would be a **minor** release change.

**V13.2.4** (wording update to add "at a global level"):

"_Verify that an allowlist is used to define, at a global level, the external resources or systems with which the application is permitted to communicate (e.g., for outbound requests, data loads, or file access). This allowlist can be implemented at the application layer, web server, firewall, or a combination of different layers._"

This is a clarification of existing intent, so should be a **patch** change.

### For a major release

Move the revised V1.3.6 to **V15.3 Defensive Coding** (renumbered appropriately), alongside 15.3.2.

### Summary of the distinction

- **V1.3.6 / future V15.3 requirement (1st layer):** Application code validates user-supplied outbound destinations against a per-feature allowlist (e.g., "for this webhook callback, only allow verified domains").
- **V13.2.4 (2nd layer):** Allowlist restricts globally which external resources the application can communicate with. As @elarlang noted, this is essential even when 1.3.6 is satisfied, because vulnerabilities can arise from functionality that is not designed to make outbound requests.

I would keep both as L2 for now. I take your point about L1 for the application-level requirement @elarlang, but I would prefer not to change levels as part of this issue.

I think the next step is to wait for the outcome of #3335 before finalising the V1.3.6 wording, since it directly affects how we handle the sanitization language. In the meantime, the V13.2.4 clarification ("at a global level") could proceed independently as a patch change.

@elarlang @jmanico, does this summary work?
I think this is an excellent resolution. Nice work Josh.
